response: ## The finding `crimes_00001` — **SVG With Embedded Raster**, high severity, confidence 0.95, on `src/assets/partner-logo.svg`. Straight from the evidence: > - **"2 `` occurrences"** > - **"embedded MIME types: image/jpeg, image/png"** > - "SVG byte size: 592 bytes (includes the base64 overhead)" So: **two** embedded rasters, MIME types **`image/jpeg`** and **`image/png`**. ## What's actually in the file `src/assets/partner-logo.svg` is a `200 × 80` canvas holding nothing but two 80×80 raster tiles and a ``: - `partner-logo.svg:3` — `<image x="0" y="0" width="80" height="80" href="data:image/png;base64,…">` - `partner-logo.svg:4` — `<image x="100" y="0" width="80" height="80" xlink:href="data:image/jpeg;base64,…">` There is **zero vector geometry** — no `<path>`, `<rect>`, `<circle>`, or `<text>`. The `.svg` extension is currently a container format, not a vector format, which is exactly what the detector is calling out. Two things worth noting while you're in here: 1. **`xlink:href` on line 4 is unbound.** The root element declares `xmlns` but not `xmlns:xlink`. In a strict XML parser that's a namespace error, and `xlink:href` has been deprecated in favour of plain `href` since SVG 2 regardless. This one gets fixed for free by the refactor. 2. Both base64 payloads decode to **1×1 pixel stubs** — this is fixture artwork standing in for the real thing. The remediation plan below is written against what those slots represent (a mark and a photographic panel); apply the same decision rule to the real payloads. ## The decision rule: vector vs. external raster Decode each payload and look at what it actually contains, because MIME type is a decent first-pass proxy: | Payload | Content type | Verdict | |---|---|---| | `image/png` @ `x=0` | Flat-colour mark / wordmark / icon — bounded palette, hard edges, no gradients | **Re-author as vector paths** | | `image/jpeg` @ `x=100` | Photographic or continuous-tone — JPEG is a lossy photo codec; nobody exports a flat logo mark as JPEG on purpose | **Split out to a standalone raster asset** | The PNG slot is the one that should become geometry. The JPEG slot almost certainly cannot be vectorised faithfully — auto-tracing a photograph produces thousands of path nodes that render slower and look worse than the original. Externalise it instead. ## Concrete remediation steps **1. Extract both payloads to disk so you can see them.** ```bash cd evals/fixtures/01-messy-ts-app/src/assets # strip the data: prefix and decode python3 - <<'PY' import base64, re, pathlib svg = pathlib.Path('partner-logo.svg').read_text() for i, (mime, b64) in enumerate(re.findall(r'data:image/(\w+);base64,([^"]+)', svg)): pathlib.Path(f'extracted-{i}.{mime}').write_bytes(base64.b64decode(b64)) PY file extracted-* ``` **2. Re-author the PNG mark as vector paths.** Preference order: - **Best:** go back to the design source (Figma / Illustrator / Sketch) and re-export the mark as SVG with *"Outline text"* on and *"Embed images"* **off**. Vendor brand kits almost always ship an authentic `.svg`; ask the partner for theirs before tracing anything. - **Fallback:** trace it — `potrace` for single-colour, `vtracer` for multi-colour — then hand-clean the node count. Only acceptable if the mark is genuinely flat-colour. The result is a `<path d="…">` (or a small group of them) sitting directly in `partner-logo.svg`, with the fill declared as a real colour rather than baked into pixels. **3. Split the JPEG out to its own asset.** Write it to `src/assets/partner-photo.webp` (or `.avif`), sized to the dimensions it actually renders at — 80×80 CSS px, so export at 160×160 for 2× DPI and stop there. WebP/AVIF over the original JPEG buys you 25–50% at equal quality, and this fixture already has an `oversized_raster` finding on `hero-banner.png` (`crime_00011`), so the same re-encode habit pays twice. **4. Rewrite the SVG to reference it.** Post-refactor the file looks like: ```svg <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="200" height="80" viewBox="0 0 200 80" role="img" aria-labelledby="partner-logo-title"> <title id="partner-logo-title">Partner logo ``` Note `href`, not `xlink:href` — that clears the unbound-namespace problem from line 4. **5. If the photo must stay inline, don't use SVG for it.** An external `href` inside an SVG doesn't resolve when the SVG is inlined via CSS `background-image` or a `data:` URI, and some email clients block it. If that's your delivery context, the right answer is *not* to re-embed base64 — it's to drop the SVG wrapper for the composite and compose in markup instead: ```html ``` That gives the browser two independently cacheable, independently compressible assets, and the mark stays resolution-independent. ## Files after the refactor | File | Role | |---|---| | `src/assets/partner-logo.svg` | **Kept and re-authored** — vector `` for the mark, one `href` reference for the photo. Still ships. | | `src/assets/partner-photo.webp` | **New** — the ex-JPEG panel, resized to render dimensions, modern codec | | `src/assets/partner-mark.svg` | *Optional* — only if you take the markup-composition route in step 5 | Nothing is deleted. `partner-logo.svg` keeps its path and its consumers; it just stops lying about being vector. ## Verifying the fix ```bash grep -c 'base64' src/assets/partner-logo.svg # expect 0 npx crimes scan --format json | jq '.findings[] | select(.type == "svg_with_embedded_raster")' ``` `crime_00001` should disappear. The detector's own suggested action agrees with the split above — *"Re-export the SVG from the design tool with the raster layer flattened to vector geometry, or split the embedded image out to its own PNG / WebP asset referenced by URL"* — at `risk: low`, `effort: small`. Its `blast_radius` is 0 and `churn` is 0, so this is an isolated, low-consequence change; the only real gate is sourcing authentic vector artwork for the mark rather than tracing a bitmap and calling it vector.
